planting.note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in wet to saturated, acidic (pH 3.5-5.5), nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum bog medium in full sun; keep standing in a tray of pure rain water or distilled water 1-2 inches deep year-round — never fertilize and never use tap water.

directions: Pale pitcher plant is the characteristic Sarracenia of the longleaf pine savannas and bogs of the western Gulf Coastal Plain, native from the Florida Panhandle through Louisiana, Texas, and southern Arkansas, distinguished by pale yellow-green to cream pitchers with fine reddish veining and a broad, wavy-edged, hood-like lid that helps keep rain out of the trap. Like its relatives, it lures insects with nectar-like secretions along the pitcher rim, and prey slide down the slick, downward-hair-lined interior into digestive fluid at the base. Nodding, cream to pale yellow flowers with a faint sweet fragrance appear on separate leafless stalks in early spring, ahead of or alongside the season's first pitchers. As the most naturally Gulf Coast-adapted pitcher plant species, it tolerates the region's hot, humid summers particularly well and is an excellent choice for a home bog garden in zone 7b-9, needing only pure water, full sun, and nutrient-poor, consistently wet acidic soil — never fertilize or plant in ordinary garden soil, both of which quickly kill Sarracenia.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or plantlets in spring in constantly wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peat/sand bog medium in partial shade; keep the medium saturated year-round with pure rain or distilled water — never fertilize and never use tap water.

directions: Southern butterwort is a small carnivorous rosette plant native to shaded seeps, spring runs, and streambanks of the Gulf Coastal Plain from Florida to Louisiana, growing in the dappled shade at the wetter, cooler edge of the bog habitats where sun-loving Sarracenia and Drosera thrive in full sun. Its pale yellow-green leaves are coated with a sticky, glistening mucilage that traps small insects such as gnats and springtails, which the leaf surface then slowly digests with secreted enzymes — the leaves can also curl slightly around larger prey to increase contact with the digestive glands. In spring it produces charming, upward-facing, pale lavender to white flowers with a yellow throat on slender stalks well above the foliage. Uniquely among North American butterworts, it readily produces small plantlets along the tips and margins of its leaves, especially where a leaf touches moist soil, making it one of the easiest carnivorous bog plants to propagate at home. Keep it constantly wet and shaded, as it is more tolerant of shade and less tolerant of full, baking sun than most other bog carnivores.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat/sand bog medium in full sun; keep the medium saturated with pure rain or distilled water year-round — never fertilize and never use tap water. Winter dormancy involves dieback to a resting bud; do not disturb the pot over winter.

directions: Tracy's sundew is a striking Gulf Coast native carnivorous plant found in the wet pine savannas and bogs of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, producing dramatically long, upright, thread-like leaves densely covered in reddish, glistening, dew-tipped glandular hairs that trap and slowly digest insects lured in by the glittering droplets. The narrow, wiry leaves can reach well over a foot tall in vigorous plants, giving the whole rosette a distinctive spidery, upright form quite unlike the low, flat rosettes of most other sundews. In late spring, tall flower stalks rise above the foliage carrying a one-sided row of showy pink blooms that open in succession over several weeks. Like other bog carnivores it demands constantly wet, nutrient-poor, acidic soil, pure water, and full sun, and it dies back to a resting bud (hibernaculum) each winter before resprouting vigorously in spring — leave the dormant crown undisturbed and keep the pot's soil from freezing solid in the colder part of its range.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)
